title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study cand-003-stud-001) that isolates downstream deterministic validation and a bounded single-repair intervention under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using a synthetic workflow stress corpus of 1,000 deterministic intents (2,000 paired episodes) and a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; any paired outcome difference can therefore arise only from downstream deterministic validation and at most one permitted repair call (guarded arm). Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired discordants n10=5 (guarded only), n01=0 (baseline only); exact two‑sided McNemar p = 0.0625 (primary preregistered confirmatory test, not < 0.05). Preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total hosted model calls recorded = 1005 (1000 shared initial + 5 repair). We present the exact McNemar as the preregistered confirmatory result, the bootstrap CI as a preregistered descriptive summary, and explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc. We interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, near‑unity baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations can reduce manual effort but introduces safety risks: misordered steps, transient invariant violations, and inadvertent protected‑field changes can convert plausible plans into risky executions. Prior empirical work documents LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that degrade code and configuration correctness, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment designed to isolate purely downstream validator and repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our principal question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate, to what degree can a deterministic validator plus at most one permitted repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes relative to reusing that same unmodified candidate (baseline)? The shared_initial_candidate design intentionally fixes first‑pass sampling so any paired difference is attributable only to deterministic validation and the permitted repair.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1,000) with deterministic task selection from a challenging synthetic NetOps workflow stress corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and explicit recording of model configuration (declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; model configuration recorded temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (3) Transparent reporting of the preregistered primary inference (exact two‑sided McNemar, p = 0.0625), preregistered descriptive bootstrap summaries (95% percentile CI = [0.001, 0.01], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an evidence‑grounded interpretation that accounts for sparse discordant counts and near‑unity baseline performance.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and controlled studies document frequent hallucinations, high prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures for code and configuration tasks; these findings motivate verifier‑augmented architectures that can catch and sometimes repair unsafe outputs [1],[2]. Work on constrained or schema‑aware decoding shows reductions in syntactic and some executable errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations are outside NetOps and rely on the fidelity of downstream validators when adapted to network workflows [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers emphasize verifier‑assisted repair, governance, and proof‑carrying proposals to mitigate automation risks; these contributions present prototypes and architectural arguments showing operational reliability depends on validator coverage and externally enforced protocols rather than on a single model alone [4],[5],[6].

Where prior studies demonstrate generate→validate→repair pipelines, evidence varies: some system and benchmark papers show measurable improvement in offline or synthetic settings, but evaluation scope and validator coverage differ across works and scenarios. Our preregistered paired comparison complements this literature by holding the initial generation constant and isolating the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation plus a single limited repair call. This avoids conflating downstream interventions with first‑pass prompt or decoding differences and clarifies the contribution and limits of validation+repair layers under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and core design. The study preregistration (study id cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation and is recorded in the archived execution manifest. Key preregistered items relevant to interpretation: confirmatory paired binary design with task_count = 1,000; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and causal interpretation. Under generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate. The guarded pipeline may deterministically reject the candidate via validation and may invoke at most one repair call but it uses the same initial candidate as baseline. Consequently, any paired outcome difference can only arise from the deterministic validator decision and the allowed repair; the design therefore does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, alternative prompts, or constrained decoding arms that were not executed.

Model/runtime configuration and temperature caveat. The declared provider/model is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The recorded model configuration shows temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Exactly one sampled initial generation per pair was reused by both arms (shared_initial_candidate). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The validator implements deterministic checks against the task manifest (required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and workflow invariants) and emits a binary safe‑deploy verdict per candidate.

Task corpus, selection rule, and validator semantics. Tasks were drawn deterministically from a synthetic challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus using the preregistered ordinal selection rule to yield exactly 1,000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains an initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (examples in representative artifacts include 'very_hard' and 'extreme'). The validator executes a deterministic digital‑twin emulation that compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints and emits structured validator traces used to score a binary valid/invalid outcome for analysis.

Execution bounds, retries, and failure treatment. The preregistration bound maximum_attempts_per_call = 1 (no retries) and required the 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment for confirmatory analysis. Execution completed without failed episodes; sensitivity analyses treating failures as unsafe were preregistered but not invoked because failed episodes = 0.

Statistical analysis plan. The preregistered confirmatory procedure is the exact two‑sided McNemar test on the 2×2 paired contingency table (n11, n10, n01, n00). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary is a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) computed by the registered analysis executor. The preregistration did not prespecify a one‑sided McNemar; any one‑sided test reported is explicitly exploratory/post‑hoc.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 2,000; completed = 2,000; complete_pairs = 1,000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call audit recorded a total of 1,005 hosted model call events: 1,000 shared initial generations and 5 repair invocations (stage counts per reconciliation). All deterministic consistency checks passed; cross‑condition cache reuse was not observed.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The observed paired contingency table: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet two‑sided α = 0.05 and therefore the preregistered H1 is not supported.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries and sensitivity. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. Because discordant counts are extremely sparse, bootstrap percentile bounds exclude zero in this run; the bootstrap was prespecified as descriptive only. An exploratory one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline), not prespecified, yields p = 0.03125 and is reported as post‑hoc/exploratory only.

Repair mechanics and representative diagnostics. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred across 1,000 pairs. Representative validator traces (archived) show the guarded pipeline rejected initial candidates for violations such as required_sequence ordering errors or protected‑interface touches and, in those five cases, invoked a single repair call that produced a repaired candidate accepted on revalidation. Representative task artifacts illustrate common patterns: required_sequence workflows (e.g., uplink failover then VLAN move), rolling access VLAN migrations, and composed redundancy/maintenance sequences. Total hosted model calls used = 1,005 (1,000 shared initial + 5 repair).

Contamination, exclusions, and missingness. Contamination checks found no prompt‑leakage flags; no post‑hoc exclusions were applied. All seeds and task_index selection rules were fixed per preregistration.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive evidence. The preregistered confirmatory result is the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625); by the preregistered decision rule this H1 is not supported at α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary that excludes zero here because bootstrap percentile methods applied to extremely sparse discordant counts can produce nonzero intervals; that descriptive statistic does not supersede the preregistered confirmatory outcome. The exploratory one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is post‑hoc and explicitly labeled exploratory.

Statistical interpretation and ceiling effects. The study preregistered a power plan assuming baseline ≈ 0.60 and a target absolute increase of 0.15; observed baseline ≈ 0.995 is far higher than assumed and thereby concentrates mass in the concordant cell n11, producing very few discordant pairs. Exact McNemar tests are discrete and sensitive to small n10/n01 counts; with n10 = 5, n01 = 0 the two‑sided exact p = 0.0625 sits just above the conventional 0.05 threshold. This outcome illustrates a ceiling‑effect phenomenon: when baseline validity is near unity, detecting small absolute gains requires either very large pair counts or designs that increase discordance (e.g., targeted injection of failure modes, independent generation arms, or expanded repair budgets).

Mechanistic implications within shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both arms began from the same sampled candidate, the observed paired improvement (n10 = 5) can only result from deterministic validator decisions and the single allowed repair. Representative validator traces show repairs addressed ordering (required_sequence) violations and protected‑field touches; these traces document concrete repair mechanics (reject→repair_prompt→candidate_recheck) for the five repaired tasks. The low repair invocation count limits inference about repair efficacy across broader failure classes: possibilities include (a) relatively few initial candidate violations in this synthetic corpus, (b) generator behavior for the declared model+prompt producing mostly valid candidates for these intents, or (c) validator rule coverage that does not capture other semantic error modalities. Distinguishing among these requires follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budget, and validator rule sets.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows verifier‑guided repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and permitted repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups we recommend (and that align with preregistered open questions) include: (1) executing independent first‑pass generation arms (not sharing initial candidates) to measure prompt/decoding intervention effects; (2) sweeping repair budgets (0..k repairs) to quantify marginal returns and repair failure‑mode coverage; (3) expanding validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity; and (4) evaluating multiple model families to map model dependence. Each follow‑up should prespecify realistic baseline failure ranges and adjust power calculations to the expected operating regime.

Threats to validity. Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate downstream effects but preclude measuring prompt/decoding interventions. External validity: the synthetic corpus and single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization to heterogeneous production environments and other model families. Conclusion validity: extreme baseline success yields sparse discordant counts, reducing power for exact paired tests and causing discrete p‑value behavior.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total hosted model calls recorded = 1,005. The preregistered confirmatory result remains the exact McNemar outcome; the paired bootstrap CI and exploratory one‑sided test are reported as descriptive and post‑hoc respectively. These artifact‑grounded results show that downstream validator/repair safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflows, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Preregistered follow‑ups should vary generator semantics, repair budgets, validator coverage, and model families and align power calculations to plausible baseline failure prevalences.

This visualization supplements the preregistered exact McNemar confirmatory test and illustrates bootstrap sensitivity to sparse discordant counts.

disclosure_statement: Declared model and provider: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). Orchestration and validator: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the validator/digital twin. Preregistration: study cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls and recorded in the archived execution manifest). Immutable initial master prompt reference archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Model configuration recorded temperature = null/unset (null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling or temperature = 0). Human role and autonomy boundary: after the autonomy lock the research run executed the preregistered experiment, analysis, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
